newsitem.title: USA: Ford pact sets job precedents, may hurt GM.
newsitem.headline: Ford pact sets job precedents, may hurt GM.

text.p: Ford Motor Co.'s labor pact with the United Auto Workers sets new precedents for preserving jobs that could spell serious trouble for General Motors Corp., analysts said Tuesday.

Based on details that have trickled out since the deal was struck Monday, analysts said the three-year pact looked like a major victory for the union beacause of Ford's committment to maintain employment for 95 percent of its 105,000-member hourly UAW work force.
The deal for the first time puts explicit limits on an automaker's ability to shrink its work force, but contained outs for Detroit's No. 2 automaker.
Analysts said the agreement, if enforced as the industry pattern, will cause serious difficulties for GM.
"On the surface, it's a little more generous than I'd like to see, not only for Ford but for Chrysler and especially GM," said J.P. Morgan auto analyst David Bradley.

According to union and industry sources, Ford must maintain a national workforce of nearly 100,000 people, with local restrictions to help protect its 49 U.S. parts and assembly plants from job losses.

To meet its commitment, Ford will have to replace thousands of employees due to retire over the next several years. The job guarantee is a wash for Ford because it does not plan to shrink its workforce, analysts said.
Analysts said Chrysler Corp. can likely afford to swallow the contract, but GM cannot.

The world's largest automaker needs to shed 50,000 to 60,000 jobs over the next several years to reach Ford's level of productivity, and the contract would severely restrict GM's ability to shrink its workforce, said Lehman Brothers auto analyst Joseph Phillippi.
"It certainly doesn't look like something GM could ever sign," Phillippi said. "They've got to be going nuts over this."
GM Chairman Jack Smith declined to comment directly on the agreement Tuesday, but noted that GM and Ford have different needs.

"Obviously General Motors is a different company than Ford," Smith said, adding that UAW President Stephen Yokich "believes it's a contract that will work for all three companies, and we'll just have to see how that works out."
It was unclear Tuesday whether the UAW would bargain with GM or the Chrysler next. The decision partly depends on whether Canadian Auto Workers union strikes Chrysler plants in Canada.
Analysts said Yokich may be willing to cut a more lenient deal for GM to help it turn around.

Both Ford and the union have refused to confirm any details of the agreement, which the union's executive board was scheduled to consider in a meeting Tuesday. The UAW's Ford Council, made up of plant-level leaders, was expected to vote on the pact Wednesday.
The Ford deal also offers generous improvements in economic benefits to workers, including a $2,000 bonus in the first year, and base-wage increases of 3 percent in the final two years.

The deal also includes significantly improved pension benefits, a key demand by many Ford workers expected to retire soon. The monthly payment rises to up to $2,260 a month from an average of $2,030 currently.
Yokich said Monday that ratification by Ford's rank-and-file workers was expected by Sept. 29.

"From what I've seen of the agreement, I can support it," said Carl Dowell, president of UAW Local 862 at Ford's Truck plants in Louisville, Ky. "It's another stop closer to preserving jobs in this country and in the plants, not shipping them out to non-union shops."
But Ford didn't open its coffers for nothing in return.
Sources said the automaker will benefit from a new, lower wage at parts plants for new work that Ford takes back from outside suppliers -- setting a precedent that the UAW has resisted for years.
The automaker also got to keep its "grow-in" period for new hires, who start at 70 percent of the full $19-an-hour wage and reach parity with veteran workers after three years.
Analysts and sources said they also believed the pact contains some hidden benefits that will allow Ford to maintain its competitiveness and flexibility.
A union source, however, said the company did not gain greater flexibility to shift parts production to outside suppliers, a process known as outsourcing.
